'''Shoumogu''' (聖母宮) is a [[Shinto shrine]] located in [[Iki, Nagasaki|Iki City]], Nagasaki Prefecture, in Katsumoto Town. Listed in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]], it is considered a potential site of the Shikinaisha "Nakatsu Shrine." However, another shrine currently bearing that name exists separately ([[Nakatsu Shrine (Iki)]]).

== Enshrined Deities ==
The shrine honors the following deities:
* [[Empress Jingū]] (Empress Jingū)
* [[Emperor Chūai]] (Emperor Chūai)
* [[Uwatsutsunoo no Mikoto]], [[Nakatsutsunoo no Mikoto]], and [[Sokotsutsunoo no Mikoto]] (collectively known as [[Sumiyoshi sanjin|Sumiyoshi Sanjin]])

The shrine is associated with Empress Jingū's [[Three Han Campaign]] (conquest of the Three Han States). Known as a deity of victory due to her triumph, she is also venerated as a deity of safe childbirth, as she gave birth to Emperor Ōjin after her victorious return.

== History ==
In the 9th year of Emperor Chūai's reign (possibly 200 CE), Empress Jingū constructed a temporary palace ([[kinzai]]) in Iki while awaiting favorable winds for her campaign. The area was named "Kazamoto" (Wind Origin) after the northward winds blew. Upon her victorious return in December of the same year, the area was renamed "Katsumoto" (Victory Origin). According to legend, 101,500 enemy heads were buried here.

The palace fell into disuse until a miraculous event involving glowing objects from the sea led to the offering of mirrors and the enshrinement of Empress Jingū. In 717 CE (Yōrō 1), the shrine was formally established, and structures were built to pray for national protection. Over time, it gained prominence as one of Iki's Seven Great Shrines and the second shrine of Iki Province. It also maintained strong connections to [[Kashii-gū|Kashii Shrine]] in Fukuoka.

Despite historical disputes regarding its status as a Shikinaisha, many researchers and reports, such as the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Shikinaisha]], suggest that Shoumogu is the original Nakatsu Shrine, while the current Nakatsu Shrine represents a later branch.

The shrine's name "Seibo" (Holy Mother) and its location in Nagasaki Prefecture often lead to misconceptions about connections with Christianity, but it is entirely unrelated.

== Festivals ==
The annual festival spans five days and is Iki's largest event. It includes the Goshinkō-sen, a boat procession listed as a [[Intangible Folk Cultural Properties Requiring Documentation|Selected Intangible Folk Cultural Property]], which predicts harvests and catches for the coming year. On October 14, the final day, events such as the Daikagura (Great Kagura Dance) of Iki and a costume parade are held. The Katsumoto Port Festival on October 15 is often considered part of the shrine's festivities, extending the celebration to six days.

== Grounds ==
The shrine grounds feature a horseshoe stone believed to bear the hoofprint of Empress Jingū's horse during the Three Han campaign. It is also historically significant as the landing site of the Mongol invasions during the [[Battle of Bun'ei]].

The main gate was donated by [[Katō Kiyomasa]] during Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Korean campaigns. The surrounding stone walls were constructed under Katō's orders as his troops awaited favorable winds, reflecting the shrine's deep ties to maritime events.
